articles.title: Plans for Scout Moor Wind Farm Reduced to 12 Turbines Amid Local Opposition
articles.excerpt: Cubico Sustainable Investments has revised its plans for the Scout Moor wind farm, reducing the number of turbines from 17 to 12, but local campaigners remain opposed to the project due to environmental concerns.
articles.content_html:
Cubico Sustainable Investments has announced a reduction in the size of its proposed Scout Moor wind farm, located on moorland between Rochdale and Bury. The initial plan for 17 wind turbines has been scaled back to 12, a move that the company claims will still provide enough energy to power approximately 84,552 homes annually, down from the previously estimated 100,000 homes.

Despite the reduction, local campaigners from the Say NO to Scout Moor 2 group continue to oppose the project. They argue that the turbines, which could reach heights of up to 180 metres including the blade tip, would dominate the skyline and be larger than Blackpool Tower. The group has been vocal in its objections since the project was first proposed in 2024.

In addition to the turbine reduction, Cubico has committed to a peat restoration project, aiming to mitigate the environmental impact of the excavation required for the wind farm. The company states that the clean energy generated will recover the fossil fuel costs associated with construction within 18 months and that peat excavation will be reduced by 28%. However, local objectors remain sceptical about the feasibility of these promises.

The planning documents indicate that the new wind farm will operate separately from the existing Scout Moor wind farm and is expected to have a lifespan of around 40 years. The project will also require underground cables to connect to an on-site substation, which will link to a supply point in Rossendale to deliver electricity to the National Grid. As the situation develops, further discussions and assessments are anticipated regarding the environmental implications and community responses to the revised plans.

articles.title: Turner Brothers Factory in Rochdale Set for Cleanup as Redevelopment Plans Progress
articles.excerpt: The derelict Turner Brothers factory in Rochdale is set to undergo a cleanup, marking a significant step towards potential redevelopment, according to the current landowners, Spodden Park Ltd.
articles.content_html:
The former Turner Brothers factory, once the world's largest asbestos manufacturer, is poised for a cleanup, which is seen as a crucial milestone in its redevelopment. The site, located in the Spotland area of Rochdale, has been derelict for decades and is often referred to as 'Rochdale's Chernobyl' due to its dangerous condition and history of asbestos production.

Spodden Park Ltd, which took control of the 75-acre site from ESG Trading Limited in 2024, has announced that they have signed a contractor to begin the remediation process. This decision comes after numerous failed attempts at redevelopment over the years, with local residents expressing a long-held desire to see the site transformed into a community asset.

While specific plans for the site have yet to be disclosed, it is understood that the new owners aim to create a park and housing, although the number of homes proposed will be significantly lower than the 650 previously suggested in earlier plans from the 2000s. The landowners have emphasised their commitment to safety, particularly given the carcinogenic nature of the materials previously handled at the factory.

Once the cleanup is completed, the site will be made viable for development, which could lead to a revitalisation of the area and provide much-needed green space for the community. The timeline for the cleanup and subsequent redevelopment remains unclear, but this announcement is a positive step forward for local residents who have long awaited action on the site.

articles.title: Why does Rochdale say ‘cruckle’?
articles.excerpt: A short guide to the little local verb — what it means, where it comes from and why Rochdale speakers keep it alive.
articles.summary: A short guide to the little local verb — what it means, where it comes from and why Rochdale speakers keep it alive.
articles.body:
If you grew up in parts of Rochdale you might have heard someone complain “I cruckled my ankle” — a quick, recognisable way of saying you’ve rolled or twisted your ankle. The word cruckle is small, local and sonorous, but it has a clear history and a place in both older dialect records and modern studies of Greater Manchester speech.

What does cruckle mean? Contemporary speakers in and around Rochdale use it to mean slipping or rolling the ankle (the little twist that makes you limp for a moment). That use matches the wider semantic field reported in historical dialect sources: an older verb recorded as crookle (and spelled variously crookle, crookl, cruckl in different records) carried senses such as ‘to make crooked’, ‘to bend, twist’ or to stoop and hobble — senses that easily cover bending, limping or crouching actions. The English Dialect Dictionary (Joseph Wright, late 19th–early 20th century) records crookle with these meanings across northern and midland counties, showing the word is not a modern invention but part of an older dialect family.

Is cruckle uniquely Rochdalian? People in the borough treat it as a Rochdale speciality, and folk memory certainly pins it to the town. Linguistic fieldwork and recent perceptual-dialect research supports that local association: a 2024 perceptual-dialect study of Greater Manchester notes ‘cruckle’ appearing in respondents’ comments when participants described Rochdale speech, alongside other locally relevant terms. That kind of folk‑linguistic evidence shows that, whether or not the root word once had wider currency, the modern label is strongly associated with Rochdale in people’s mental maps of the area’s speech.

Where does the word come from? Dialectists trace cruckle/crookle to predictable patterns in northern English and Scots dialects: an imitative or onomatopoeic root (crook-/krug-) meaning ‘bend, hook’ plus a frequentative or verbalising element (‑le) that creates verbs for small or repeated motions (so crook → crookle → cruckle). Comparable forms turn up in Scots and north‑Atlantic dialect records (the Dictionary of the Scots Language records cruggle/cruckle/krukel with senses like ‘to crouch’ or ‘to huddle’), suggesting the word belongs to an old, regionally distributed family of verbs rather than being an isolated modern coinage.

What can dialect research tell us about cruckle? Three things are useful to bear in mind. First, historical dictionaries like Joseph Wright’s English Dialect Dictionary document earlier meanings and spellings and show that the form has long been present in northern English. Second, descriptive work such as the Scottish dialect dictionaries records cognate forms with related senses, which helps linguists reconstruct how meanings and forms travelled and changed across neighbouring speech communities. Third, contemporary perceptual and folk‑linguistic studies — the kind that ask residents to name words they associate with a place — reveal how small words become identity markers: even if a word has older relatives elsewhere, its strong contemporary link to a town like Rochdale tells us about local pride, memory and how speakers use vocabulary to signal belonging.

How confident can we be about any single claim? The historical record and modern academic study give a clear, checkable trail: crookle/cruckle appears in primary dialect sources from the 19th and early 20th centuries, Scots dialect materials record closely related forms, and recent perceptual‑dialect research shows locals link the term to Rochdale today. At the same time, much evidence of local use comes from speakers’ reports and oral tradition; that is legitimate linguistic data, but it is different from formal dictionary quotations or published fieldwork. If you have family examples, written notes or dated usages from Rochdale (old letters, school logs, parish notes), local archives and dialect projects welcome them — those small, dated records are exactly the material researchers need to trace change with precision.

So: why does Rochdale say cruckle? Because the town’s speech keeps alive a small verb from an older northern dialect family, and because local speakers use that word as a familiar shorthand for a particular, everyday stumble. The result is a tiny, useful piece of local identity — a word that tells you not just what happened to somebody’s foot, but where they’re from.

Rochdale will host Swindon Town in a League Two match at the Crown Oil Arena on Saturday, 3 October 2026. The match is significant for both teams as they look to improve their positions in the league table during a congested fourth tier season.

Rochdale comes into the match with a positive momentum, having secured seven points from their last three games, including two consecutive victories. In contrast, Swindon Town is struggling, currently on a three-game winless streak, making this match crucial for both sides.

articles.title: Rochdale Council Refuses Office Use Application for Bridge House on Mellor Street
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council has rejected an application to certify six offices at Bridge House, Mellor Street, due to lack of evidence supporting their use as offices.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has refused an application for a certificate of lawfulness concerning six offices at Bridge House, Mellor Street, citing a lack of evidence that the building has been used as offices. The application was submitted by Shahida Farooq, who claimed that the property had operated as commercial offices for over ten years, which would typically qualify it for such a certificate.

The planning officer's report highlighted that the building, located between Mellor Street and Spotland Road, had previously been used for a private-hire booking office and light industrial purposes, both of which had received planning permission. The report noted that there have been three planning applications associated with the site, with the most recent being in 1999 for the use of the basement as a private-hire booking office.

Images from Google Streetview taken in August 2016 show that the front of the building featured two units, with signage indicating the presence of an accountancy service and a conservatory and garden furniture business. These findings contributed to the council's decision to reject the application, as there was insufficient evidence to support the claim of office use.

The refusal means that the current status of the building remains unchanged, and it will not be classified as having lawful office use. It is unclear what steps, if any, Mrs Farooq may take next regarding this decision.

articles.title: Plans for Heat Network Using Waste Heat from Local Industries Announced for Greater Manchester
articles.excerpt: A new initiative aims to create a heat network across Greater Manchester, utilising waste heat from various sources, including a baked beans factory in Wigan and a distribution centre in Rochdale, potentially reducing energy bills significantly.
articles.content_html:
A major initiative is being proposed to create a heat network across Greater Manchester, which could power thousands of homes using waste heat from sources such as baked beans, sewage, and data centres. EnergiRaven, a UK-based green energy consultancy, is pitching this plan to local councils, aiming to establish a network of pipes that would transport captured heat to residential areas, potentially reducing energy bills by up to 38%.

The project, informally referred to as the 'Bee Network for Heat', is inspired by a successful publicly-owned model in Denmark that has been operational for decades. A map of the proposed network indicates that heat could be sourced from various locations, including the Baked Beans factory in Wigan, a bread factory near Bolton, and Asda's distribution centre in Rochdale. Additionally, heat from data centres, wastewater treatment works, and the Carrington Power Plant is also being considered.

At a recent event on September 30, it was highlighted that a data centre in Heywood could provide enough heat for approximately 50,000 homes. EnergiRaven estimates that the heat network could meet 85% of the region's heating needs, potentially saving households around £8.83 billion over the next 20 years. Currently, heating costs are around 8.7p per kWh, but this could decrease to 5.4p with the implementation of the network.

The initiative aims to protect homes from energy price shocks, particularly in light of recent global conflicts affecting energy supplies. While the project will require investment, it is seen as a sustainable solution to rising energy costs, which have surged significantly in the UK. The UK government spent £39.3 billion on energy subsidies between October 2022 and March 2023, highlighting the urgent need for alternative energy solutions.

articles.title: Barbara Gould Retires After 34 Years as Middleton's Lollipop Lady
articles.excerpt: Barbara Gould, a beloved lollipop lady in Middleton, has completed her final crossing after 34 years of service, ensuring the safety of schoolchildren in the area.
articles.content_html:
Barbara Gould has retired after 34 years of service as a lollipop lady in Middleton, helping schoolchildren cross the road for the final time today. Since 1992, she has been a familiar presence at various schools, including St Michael’s Primary School, St Thomas More, Alkrington Primary, Middleton Technology School, and St Peter’s Primary School.

Councillor Dylan Williams, Rochdale Council Cabinet Member for Highways and Facilities, praised Barbara's dedication on social media, recalling how she had helped him cross the road during his own childhood. He expressed gratitude for her long-standing commitment to the community and wished her a happy retirement.

Local residents also shared their appreciation for Barbara's service. Patricia Locke commented, "Happy retirement Barbara. Thank you for keeping the children safe when crossing the road."

Barbara's retirement marks the end of an era for many families in Middleton, as she has been a key figure in ensuring the safety of children commuting to school for over three decades.

articles.title: Rochdale Entrepreneur Launches Gift Guide for Outdoor Enthusiasts
articles.excerpt: Sophie Ahmed, founder of Alley Crafters, has introduced an online gift guide aimed at helping shoppers find meaningful presents for walkers and hikers, addressing a common gifting dilemma.
articles.content_html:
A local entrepreneur from Rochdale has launched a new initiative designed to assist shoppers in finding the perfect gifts for outdoor enthusiasts. Sophie Ahmed, the founder of Alley Crafters, has created an online gift guide specifically tailored for walkers and hikers, which aims to simplify the often challenging task of selecting thoughtful presents for those who already possess a wide array of outdoor gear.

The guide, titled '25 Gifts for Walkers & Hikers UK', features a curated selection of practical and unique items that outdoor lovers are likely to appreciate. It includes suggestions such as OS maps, walking memberships, head torches, insulated flasks, and personalised gifts inspired by memorable walks and locations. This resource is intended to inspire shoppers with creative yet functional ideas for any occasion.

Sophie Ahmed's initiative was born out of her own experiences and frustrations when trying to find meaningful gifts for passionate hikers. By focusing on practical items that can be used on the trails, the guide aims to cut through the clutter of generic outdoor gear and provide shoppers with a more personalised gifting experience.

The launch of this gift guide is expected to resonate with those looking for unique presents for outdoor lovers, whether they are casual walkers or seasoned fell-walkers. The guide is now available online, making it easier for shoppers to access and explore the various gifting options.

articles.title: Oldham to Rochdale Tram Line Reopens Following Track Replacement
articles.excerpt: Tram services have resumed on the Oldham to Rochdale line after essential track replacement work was completed, part of a £150m investment in Greater Manchester's tram network.
articles.content_html:
Tram services have resumed on the Oldham to Rochdale line after essential track replacement work was successfully completed. This marks a significant milestone in the summer programme of network improvements aimed at enhancing the Greater Manchester tram system.

The work involved a planned two-week closure between Victoria and Rochdale town centre and is part of a wider £150 million investment to maintain and improve the tram network. Engineers worked around the clock to replace 1.2 kilometres of track, improve drainage, renew foundations, and correct the alignment and level of the track. This complex operation utilised approximately 290 new concrete sleepers, 2,000 tonnes of gravel, and over 5,000 tonnes of ballast.

As a result of the improvements, sections of the route that previously required speed restrictions can now operate at normal speeds of up to 50 mph, which is expected to enhance journey times for passengers. Ian Davies, Network Director for Metrolink at Transport for Greater Manchester (TfGM), stated that this engineering work will significantly improve the reliability and long-term condition of the network.

Further improvement work is scheduled to take place at various locations across the Bee Network in the coming months, with significant projects planned at Trafford Bar and Deansgate-Castlefield. During this time, there will be no trams on the Eccles, Trafford Centre, or Altrincham lines for three weeks from Monday, 13th July to Sunday, 2nd August.

A 36-year-old man from Heywood has been handed a suspended 30-month prison sentence for possessing cocaine with intent to supply. Joshua Carroll, of Peel Lane, pleaded guilty to the charges at Manchester Magistrates’ Court on September 1, 2026, with the offences occurring in Rochdale on July 1, 2022.

The sentencing took place at Manchester Crown Court on September 29, 2026. The court suspended the sentence for two years, meaning Carroll will avoid custody if he adheres to the conditions set by the court. He is required to complete 150 hours of unpaid work and pay £150 in prosecution costs along with a £228 surcharge.

In addition to the suspended sentence, the court ordered the forfeiture and destruction of drugs and related items seized during the investigation. Carroll was also ordered to forfeit £21,141.71 in cash linked to the drug offences. He will be under supervision for two years as part of his sentence, and a collection order mandates that he make payments by March 29, 2027.

This case highlights ongoing efforts to combat drug-related crime in the area. Local residents may see continued police activity as authorities work to address drug supply issues in Rochdale and surrounding areas.

articles.title: Renovation of College Bank's Seven Sisters Towers Could Take Over a Decade
articles.excerpt: Housing chiefs have stated that renovating the Seven Sisters tower blocks in College Bank would displace residents for more than ten years, as discussions continue on the future of the iconic buildings.
articles.content_html:
Housing chiefs have warned that renovating the Seven Sisters tower blocks in College Bank could take more than a decade, displacing residents for the entire duration of the work. This statement comes as Rochdale Boroughwide Housing (RBH) has yet to make a decision regarding the future of the iconic buildings, which have been a part of Rochdale's skyline for 61 years.

Residents have expressed their desire for refurbishment rather than demolition and have sought support from Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig. The scale of the renovation required to bring the buildings up to modern standards is significant, and RBH has indicated that the blocks would not be habitable until the work is completed.

The discussion around the future of College Bank began in earnest in 2017, when RBH first raised concerns about the buildings nearing the end of their life. In response, tenants formed the Save the Seven Sisters campaign, hoping to see the towers restored through a partnership between RBH and Legal and General Affordable Homes. However, this partnership was dissolved in September 2024, leading to further uncertainty for residents.

In November 2024, a Mayoral Taskforce was established to explore options for the College Bank estate. Recent surveys conducted by RBH revealed that the blocks are not safe for continued occupation, necessitating the relocation of residents. As discussions progress, the future of the Seven Sisters remains uncertain, with the community keenly awaiting a resolution.

articles.title: Are there really fairies in Healey Dell?
articles.excerpt: A look at the rock niche called the Fairies’ Chapel, the documentary history of Healey Dell and how 19th‑century storytellers turned landscape into legend.
articles.summary: A look at the rock niche called the Fairies’ Chapel, the documentary history of Healey Dell and how 19th‑century storytellers turned landscape into legend.
articles.body:
Healey Dell is one of this borough’s best‑known beauty spots: a steep, wooded stretch of the River Spodden with waterfalls, industrial‑archaeology remains and a striking Victorian viaduct. The site is managed as a local nature reserve and promoted locally for wildlife, walks and family trails. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

Documented history

The clearest, verifiable facts are straightforward. The most visible man‑made landmark is the Healey Dell (or Spodden Valley) viaduct, a stone railway viaduct built in 1869–70 now recorded on the National Heritage List for England (Grade II). That listing records the viaduct’s date and architectural features and is the official source for its historic status. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1317784))

Healey Dell is also recognised locally for its wildlife and industrial remains: former mill sites, reservoirs and the disused Rochdale‑to‑Bacup railway line that became a walking route. The patchwork of conservation designations and local management explains why the Dell has been preserved and interpreted for visitors rather than being redeveloped; local authority material and planning records identify the area as a Local Nature Reserve and a valued Site of Biological Importance. Where administrative or planning details are time‑sensitive (for example management plans or conservation grants), the public record on council and planning sites should be checked for the latest dates and decisions. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

Folklore and the Fairies’ Chapel

The “Fairies’ Chapel” is a small rock niche and cascade on the River Spodden, a feature visitors have long noticed because the hollowed rock and its small pool suggest a miniature, church‑like space. Local guides and the Healey Dell Heritage Centre acknowledge that the alcove’s appearance is the result of water‑erosion acting on the bedrock, and they also present the traditional tales that grew up around the spot. Those tales are storytelling and interpretation layered on top of the physical place, not separate documentary records of events. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/things-to-do/the-fairies-chapel/))

The best‑known written record of the tales dates to the 19th century. John Roby, a collector of Lancashire legends, printed versions of the Healey Dell stories — including the account of an enchanted chapel, a Fairy Queen and the Healey Dwarf — in his Traditions of Lancashire. Roby’s volumes are important as records of local storytelling, but they are not documentary proof of supernatural events; Roby himself compiled and reworked oral tradition and local romance for a Victorian readership. If you want the earliest printed versions of the tale, Roby is the primary source. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/15271/pg15271-images.html))

What the stories say (and what we can verify)

There are several overlapping strands in local versions: an enchanted cavern where fairies held court; a small figure sometimes called the Healey Dwarf; prophecies and encounters that befall local characters; and a dramatic episode in which witches are turned to stone. These elements are part of oral tradition and poetic retellings and are preserved in Victorian collections and modern retellings by local heritage groups. They are folklore—useful for understanding local culture and Victorian taste in storytelling—but they are not reducible to verifiable events in the historical record. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/15271/pg15271-images.html))

How the Dell uses the stories today

Local interpretation deliberately keeps both threads — the real, documentable history and the folkloric — visible. The heritage centre, council walking guides and family trails present the Fairies’ Chapel as a natural feature with a storytelling past: a way to engage visitors, especially children, with nature and local memory. If you are looking for archival evidence that fairies or witch‑turnings actually occurred, none exists in the way a historian would accept; what exists instead are printed and oral traditions and the physical niche that inspired them. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/things-to-do/the-fairies-chapel/))

If you visit

Treat the Fairies’ Chapel as you would any feature of local heritage: enjoy the setting, respect the riverside ecology, and remember that much of what makes the Dell magical is human imagination shaped by landscape. For anyone curious about the sources behind the stories, the 19th‑century collections and the council and heritage centre materials are the best starting points — Roby for the printed tradition, Historic England and the council for the site’s verifiable history. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/15271/pg15271-images.html))

articles.title: Hopwood Hall Volunteer Expresses Disappointment Over High Court Ruling
articles.excerpt: A long-standing volunteer at Hopwood Hall has shared their disappointment regarding the recent High Court ruling affecting the estate, highlighting their deep connection to the site and ongoing restoration efforts.
articles.content_html:
BREAKING NEWS — LIVE

Live updates, newest first.

08:46, 02 October 2026

A long-standing volunteer at Hopwood Hall has shared their disappointment following a recent High Court ruling regarding the estate, highlighting their deep connection to the historic site and ongoing restoration efforts.

08:26, 02 October 2026

A long-standing volunteer at Hopwood Hall has shared their feelings of disappointment following the recent High Court ruling regarding the estate, emphasising the personal significance of the Hall and its restoration efforts.

A volunteer with over two decades of involvement at Hopwood Hall has expressed disappointment following a recent High Court ruling concerning the estate. The volunteer, who has actively supported the restoration project since 2013, described the Hall as an integral part of their life and community.

In a letter to the editor published by the source, the volunteer recounted their first encounter with Hopwood Hall in 2003, when they discovered the boarded-up building while walking in the surrounding woods. They noted that the Hall, even in its dilapidated state, struck them as a hidden gem worth saving.

The volunteer, along with their brother, became involved in the restoration efforts initiated by Hopwood DePree, who sought to preserve his ancestral home. They participated in the early stages of the project, serving on the original committee and contributing to various restoration activities, including gardening and public engagement during open days. Their efforts were recognised through several awards, reflecting their commitment to the Hall and the community.

The letter highlights the emotional significance of Hopwood Hall to the volunteer and the community, emphasising their dedication to making visitors feel welcome and fostering a positive image of the restoration project. The outcome of the High Court proceedings has raised concerns about the future of the estate and the ongoing efforts to restore it.

articles.title: Seven Arrested in Police Raids Uncovering Cannabis Farms in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Seven individuals have been arrested after police uncovered three cannabis farms during coordinated raids across the Rochdale district, involving over 50 officers.
articles.content_html:
BREAKING NEWS — LIVE

Live updates, newest first.

08:26, 02 October 2026

Seven individuals have been arrested after police conducted early morning raids at six addresses across the Rochdale district, uncovering three cannabis farms and seizing drugs and cash.

08:17, 02 October 2026

Seven individuals have been arrested after police uncovered three cannabis farms during coordinated raids across the Rochdale district, involving over 50 officers.

07:11, 02 October 2026

A police operation across Rochdale has led to the arrest of seven individuals and the dismantling of three cannabis farms, following months of intelligence gathering.

06:39, 02 October 2026

Seven individuals have been arrested in connection with three cannabis farms discovered during police raids across Rochdale, Heywood, and Middleton. The operation involved over 50 officers and resulted in the seizure of drugs, cash, and a stolen vehicle.

04:43, 02 October 2026

Greater Manchester Police have arrested seven individuals and shut down multiple cannabis farms in a coordinated operation across Rochdale, Heywood, and Middleton.

Seven people have been arrested following a series of police raids that uncovered three cannabis farms across the Rochdale district. The operation, which involved more than 50 officers, took place early on Thursday morning and targeted six addresses in areas including Heywood, Middleton, and Newhey.

The raids were the culmination of several months of intelligence gathering by Greater Manchester Police, aimed at dismantling organised crime groups operating in the region. During the searches, police seized a significant number of cannabis plants, cash, Class A drugs, and a vehicle suspected to be stolen.

Among those arrested were a 33-year-old man and a 33-year-old woman, both suspected of cultivating cannabis and abstracting electricity. Additionally, a 61-year-old man and a 61-year-old woman were arrested on similar charges. A 35-year-old man was taken into custody on suspicion of possession with intent to supply Class A drugs, while a 28-year-old man was arrested for possession with intent to supply Class B drugs. A 78-year-old man was also arrested on suspicion of handling stolen property.

All seven individuals remain in custody for questioning as police continue their investigations. Inspector Graham Cooke stated that the operation marks a significant step in tackling organised crime in the area, emphasising the commitment of the police to disrupt criminal activities that affect local communities.
